Loopholes are readily exploited, allowing foreign entities to funnel money into political campaigns and lobbying efforts through intermediaries, obscuring the true source of the funding and hindering accountability. This ban is not about suppressing voices; it is about protecting the very foundations of American democracy from external manipulation and ensuring that the government remains truly representative of the will of the American people. #Preserving Democracy: The Necessity of a Complete Ban on Foreign Political Donations and Lobbying

Upholding National Sovereignty and Democratic Self-Governance

At its core, a functioning democracy operates on the principle of popular sovereignty—the idea that political authority resides with the people. When foreign entities inject money into U.S. elections or lobby policymakers, they undermine this principle by allowing outsiders to influence decisions that should be made solely by U.S. citizens and their elected representatives. The Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) of 1971 already prohibits foreign nationals from contributing to U.S. political campaigns, underscoring Congress’s intent to prevent external financial meddling. However, loopholes—such as funneling donations through shell corporations or influential intermediaries—persist, allowing foreign money to seep into the political system.

A total ban would eliminate these ambiguities, ensuring that U.S. policy is determined by domestic interests rather than foreign agendas. When lobbying firms in Washington advocate on behalf of foreign governments or multinational corporations, they often prioritize narrow interests over the public good. For example, foreign oil companies have historically lobbied against U.S. environmental regulations that could harm their profits, even at the expense of American communities facing climate crises. Such cases demonstrate how foreign financial influence can distort national priorities. By severing all ties between foreign entities and U.S. political actors, the nation can reclaim control over its own governance.

Preventing Corruption and Ensuring Undisputed Accountability

The corrupting influence of money in politics is a well-documented threat to democratic integrity. When foreign entities donate to U.S. campaigns, they do not do so out of altruism—they do so to gain reciprocal favors. Research has shown that lobbyists for foreign interests secure significantly more favorable policies than those who represent domestic groups. This creates a system where elected officials may owe more to foreign benefactors than to their own constituents, undermining the very concept of representative democracy.

Moreover, the appearance of corruption is nearly as damaging as actual corruption. Even if no explicit quid pro quo exists, the knowledge that foreign money flows into U.S. politics fosters distrust in government. Polls consistently show that Americans believe their politicians are more beholden to wealthy donors than to voters. A total ban on foreign financial influence would help restore faith in the system by eliminating overseas financial pressure points that distort policy outcomes.

A 2020 report by the Center for Responsive Politics found that Chinese entities (including state-backed companies and affiliated interest groups) spent over $21 million lobbying U.S. officials in just two years. Their priorities? Suppressing criticism of China’s human rights abuses, weakening U.S. support for Taiwan, and advancing trade policies favorable to Beijing. By allowing such financial entanglements to persist, the U.S. risks becoming a puppet of foreign interests rather than an independent global leader.

Safeguarding Elections from Foreign Interference

Perhaps the most immediate threat to democracy posed by foreign financial influence is electoral interference. While much attention has been given to cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns orchestrated by foreign adversaries, monetary donations represent a more insidious form of meddling. When foreign governments or corporations bankroll U.S. political campaigns, they effectively manipulate electoral outcomes to favor candidates sympathetic to their agendas.

A ban on foreign lobbying and donations would eliminate this financial leverage, reinforcing the legitimacy of U.S. elections.

Shielding the Republic: The Case for a Complete Ban on Foreign Political Donations and Lobbying

Introduction

The American democratic experiment, forged in the crucible of revolution and codified in a Constitution designed to vest sovereignty in the people, has always rested on a foundational premise: that the government of the United States answers to its citizens alone. Yet in an era of unprecedented global capital flows, transnational corporate empires, and sophisticated influence operations, this premise faces a profound and growing challenge. Foreign entities—governments, corporations, and wealthy individuals—wield an expanding arsenal of financial tools to shape American policy outcomes, distort public discourse, and compromise the independence of elected officials. A complete and enforceable ban on all political donations and lobbying activities by foreign entities is not merely a policy preference; it is an existential necessity for the preservation of democratic self-governance.

I. The Constitutional Imperative

The Founders were not naïve about the dangers of foreign influence. Indeed, their fears were among the most frequently voiced concerns at the Constitutional Convention and in the ratification debates that followed. Alexander Hamilton warned in Federalist No. 68 of the "desire in foreign powers to gain an improper ascendant in our councils." George Washington's Farewell Address remains one of the most eloquent warnings ever issued by a head of state against the "insidious wiles of foreign influence," urging the nation to "steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world."

These were not idle musings. The Founders understood, from both historical study and personal experience under British colonial rule, that a republic's sovereignty is only as strong as the integrity of its decision-making processes. When foreign money flows into the political system—whether through direct campaign contributions, bundled donations routed through domestic intermediaries, or the hiring of armies of lobbyists to press foreign interests on Capitol Hill—the practical effect is the same: American policy is shaped, at least in part, by actors who owe no allegiance to the American people and are accountable to no American electorate.

The constitutional architecture was designed to prevent precisely this. The Emoluments Clause (Article I, Section 9) prohibits officeholders from accepting payments from foreign states without congressional consent. The Logan Act (1799) criminalizes unauthorized negotiations with foreign governments. These provisions reflect a deep, bipartisan, and historically consistent understanding that foreign financial entanglements are incompatible with the functioning of an independent republic.

II. The Current Regulatory Framework: A Patchwork Riddled with Holes

To its credit, the United States has enacted certain restrictions on foreign participation in its political process. The Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA), as amended, prohibits foreign nationals from making direct or indirect contributions to federal, state, or local elections. The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (BCRA) of 2002 reinforced these prohibitions. And the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) of 1938 requires individuals acting on behalf of foreign principals to register with the Department of Justice and disclose their activities.

Yet the enforcement and scope of these laws are woefully inadequate. Consider the following gaps:

1. The Corporate Shell Game. Foreign-owned or foreign-controlled corporations can establish U.S.-based subsidiaries, and those subsidiaries can make political contributions and spend unlimited sums on political advertising through Political Action Committees (PACs) and Super PACs. The Supreme Court's decision in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) opened the floodgates to unlimited corporate spending on political communications, and the decision provided no effective mechanism to distinguish between genuinely domestic corporate political activity and that which is driven by foreign shareholders or parent companies. A 2016 report by the Campaign Legal Center documented numerous instances of foreign-connected corporations spending millions on U.S. elections with minimal scrutiny.

2. The Lobbying Loophole. While FARA requires registration by foreign agents, enforcement has historically been sporadic. A 2016 investigation by the Project on Government Oversight found that the Department of Justice had prosecuted only a handful of FARA violations in the preceding decades, even as hundreds of foreign governments and entities maintained active lobbying operations in Washington. Moreover, the Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) of 1995 provides a separate, less restrictive registration pathway that many foreign-connected lobbyists exploit, particularly when their work involves "political activities" that fall short of the narrow definitions triggering FARA obligations. The result is a shadowy ecosystem in which billions of dollars in foreign-origin funds flow through law firms, consultancies, and lobbying shops to influence legislation, regulatory decisions, and executive policy—often with minimal transparency.

3. Dark Money and Nonprofit Conduits. The rise of "dark money" organizations—501(c)(4) social welfare organizations and 501(c)(6) trade associations that can engage in political activity without disclosing their donors—has created yet another vector for foreign influence. Because these organizations are not required to reveal their funding sources, there is no effective way to determine whether foreign money is being funneled through them into the American political process. Multiple investigative reports have raised concerns that foreign funds may be entering the U.S. political system through these opaque channels, yet regulatory agencies have been slow to act.

4. Individual Wealthy Foreign Nationals. While foreign nationals are barred from direct campaign contributions, the lines become blurred when it comes to issue advocacy, independent expenditures, and political engagement through domestic entities. Wealthy foreign individuals can establish U.S.-based foundations, fund think tanks, endow university programs, and support advocacy organizations that shape policy debates in ways that benefit their home countries or personal interests—all without violating existing law. The cumulative effect of these activities can be as influential as direct campaign contributions, yet they operate in a regulatory gray zone that existing law fails to address.

III. The Scale of the Problem: Why the Stakes Are Existential

Some may argue that the current restrictions, imperfect as they are, are "good enough" and that a complete ban would be excessive. This argument fails to reckon with the scale and sophistication of modern foreign influence operations.

Geopolitical competition has intensified. The rise of strategic rivals with massive sovereign wealth funds, state-owned enterprises, and centralized political systems capable of directing private-sector activity has fundamentally changed the calculus. When the Chinese Communist Party can direct a state-owned corporation to invest in a U.S. company, and that U.S. company's PAC subsequently funds candidates sympathetic to Beijing's interests, the causal chain of foreign influence may be attenuated, but the practical effect is unmistakable. The same dynamic plays out with Gulf state sovereign wealth funds, Russian oligarchs, and other actors whose financial decisions are intertwined with their governments' strategic objectives.

The return on investment is enormous. U.S. defense spending, trade policy, sanctions decisions, technology export controls, and regulatory actions have trillion-dollar implications for foreign governments and corporations. When the cost of a lobbying campaign or a bundling operation is measured in the low millions, and the potential policy payoff is measured in the billions or even trillions, the incentive for foreign entities to invest in American political influence is overwhelming. No amount of half-measures will overcome this fundamental economic logic. Only a comprehensive ban, enforced with serious penalties and robust oversight, can close the gap.

Democratic legitimacy is at stake. Public trust in government is at historic lows. Polls consistently show that large majorities of Americans—across party lines—believe that the political system serves the interests of wealthy donors and special interests rather than ordinary citizens. Adding the perception (and reality) of foreign influence to this toxic mix is a recipe for democratic disillusionment. When citizens believe that their elected officials are responsive to foreign money rather than domestic concerns, the social contract that underpins democratic governance begins to erode.

IV. The Case for Comprehensiveness: Why Half-Measures Fail

A critical objection to a total ban is that it may be overbroad, sweeping in benign activities such as a Canadian citizen making a small donation to a local candidate, or a European trade association filing public comments on a proposed regulation. These concerns, while not frivolous, do not withstand scrutiny.

First, the principle of sovereignty demands erring on the side of exclusion. The right of foreign entities to participate in American political decision-making is not a recognized right—neither constitutionally, philosophically, nor in international law. Every sovereign nation reserves the right to limit foreign participation in its domestic political processes. The United States should be no exception. The small inconveniences that a comprehensive ban might impose on marginal actors are vastly outweighed by the systemic benefits of eliminating foreign financial influence from the political system.

Second, half-measures create loopholes that sophisticated actors will exploit. History demonstrates conclusively that partial bans, narrow definitions, and tiered regulatory frameworks are easily circumvented by well-resourced foreign interests. Any definition that permits some foreign political activity while prohibiting other activity will be gamed. Law firms will structure transactions to remain just within the boundaries of the law. Lobbyists will reclassify their activities to avoid triggering FARA registration. Corporate subsidiaries will be restructured to maximize political spending while minimizing foreign-ownership visibility. The only effective approach is a bright-line rule: no foreign entity—defined broadly to include any entity with significant foreign ownership, control, or direction—may contribute to political campaigns, fund political advertising, or lobby U.S. government officials.

Third, enforcement must be meaningful. A ban is only as strong as its enforcement mechanism. The essay argues not only for a legislative ban but for the creation of a dedicated enforcement body—perhaps an enhanced division within the Federal Election Commission or a new independent agency—empowered with investigative authority, subpoena power, and the ability to impose severe civil and criminal penalties. Fines should be calibrated to the resources of the offending entity; for a multinational corporation or a sovereign wealth fund, only penalties measured in billions will serve as a meaningful deterrent. And individuals who knowingly facilitate foreign influence—whether as bundlers, lobbyists, consultants, or corporate officers—should face personal criminal liability.

V. Addressing Counterarguments

"This will harm international business." The ban proposed here targets political activity, not commercial activity. Foreign corporations are free to operate in the United States, invest in American industry, employ American workers, and compete in American markets. What they should not be free to do is use their financial resources to shape the political rules under which they compete. The distinction is clear and defensible: commerce is welcome; political manipulation is not.

"This restricts free speech." The Supreme Court has long recognized that the government has a compelling interest in preventing foreign influence over the American political process. In Bluman v. FEC (2012), a three-judge district court (with the decision summarily affirmed by the Supreme Court) upheld the prohibition on foreign national political contributions, holding that the government's interest in limiting foreign influence is "sufficient to justify the limited burden on First Amendment rights." A comprehensive ban is a natural extension of this established principle.

"American citizens abroad will be affected." The ban targets foreign entities, not American citizens living abroad. U.S. citizens retain their full political rights regardless of residence. The ban can and should be carefully drafted to distinguish between foreign nationals and American citizens, and between foreign-controlled entities and genuinely independent American organizations.

"Other countries allow foreign participation." The comparative argument cuts the other way. Many democracies—including Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom—impose strict limits on foreign political donations and influence. The United States, as the world's most consequential democracy and the most attractive target for foreign influence, should lead, not follow, in establishing robust protections.

VI. A Bipartisan Imperative

It bears emphasizing that this is not a partisan issue. Concerns about foreign influence in American politics have been raised with equal force by Democrats and Republicans, by progressives and conservatives, by civil libertarians and national security hawks. The intelligence community has documented foreign attempts to influence American elections from multiple directions. The threat is bipartisan, and so must be the solution.

A comprehensive ban on foreign political donations and lobbying would enjoy broad public support. Polling consistently shows that Americans of all political persuasions oppose foreign interference in their elections and resent the outsized influence of money in politics. A legislative package that combines a clear prohibition, robust enforcement, and meaningful penalties would be one of the most popular and consequential reforms in a generation.

VII. Conclusion: Reclaiming Self-Governance

Democracy, at its core, is the proposition that a nation's people should govern themselves. This proposition is fatally undermined when foreign money—whether flowing from Beijing, Riyadh, Moscow, or the boardroom of a multinational corporation—distorts the political process. The American people did not fight for independence from the British Crown only to find themselves subject to the influence of a new set of foreign masters wielding checkbooks instead of muskets.

A complete ban on all political donations and lobbying activities by foreign entities is not a radical proposal. It is the logical fulfillment of the Founders' vision, the natural extension of existing law, and the only adequate response to the scale and sophistication of modern foreign influence operations. The integrity of American democracy—the principle that the government of the United States answers to the American people and to no one else—demands nothing less.

The Republic must be defended. The time to act is now.

"Sovereign Nation, Sovereign Voice"

A Speech on Banning Foreign Political Donations and Lobbying

My fellow Americans,

I stand before you today not as a partisan, not as a representative of any faction, but as a citizen who loves this republic — and who fears that its most sacred promise is under siege.

That promise is simple: We, the People, govern ourselves.

Not foreign capitals. Not multinational interests. Not the well-funded emissaries of governments who do not share our values. We decide the future of this nation — or we are supposed to.

Let me ask you a question I believe cuts to the heart of our democracy: Why should a single dollar from a foreign government, a foreign corporation, or a foreign billionaire be allowed to influence who leads us, what laws we pass, and what direction this nation takes?

I'll answer my own question: It shouldn't. Not now. Not ever.

I. The Principle of Self-Governance

The Founders of this nation did not risk their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor so that foreign powers could buy influence in the halls of Congress. They broke with a king across the ocean precisely so that Americans — and Americans alone — would determine the course of American governance.

James Madison warned us in Federalist No. 52 that representatives should owe their election to the people and no one else. Alexander Hamilton cautioned against what he called the "most pernicious" of all foreign influences — those that corrupt the deliberative process of a free nation.

These were not idle musings. They were warnings. And today, we have failed to heed them.

When foreign governments and interests funnel money into our political system — whether through direct donations, Super PACs, shell organizations, or armies of well-connected lobbyists — they are not participating in our democracy. They are hijacking it.

II. The Reality We Face

Let's be honest about what is happening.

Every single election cycle, billions of dollars course through the American political system. And buried within those billions are contributions and expenditures that trace back — sometimes directly, sometimes through carefully constructed legal veils — to foreign entities.

Foreign governments hire former members of Congress, former Cabinet officials, and former senior staffers as lobbyists. These individuals walk into the very buildings where they once served the American people, and they advocate — for a price — on behalf of foreign regimes. Some of those regimes are allies. Some are adversaries. None of them should have a seat at our table.

And it doesn't stop at lobbying. Foreign-linked money flows into think tanks that shape policy. It funds media campaigns that shape public opinion. It underwrites academic programs that shape the next generation of policymakers. The influence is systemic, pervasive, and corrosive.

Let me be blunt: This is not a partisan issue. This is not about left or right. This is about whether America is for sale — and right now, the answer is that it is. To the highest bidder.

III. The Case for an Absolute Ban

I am here to call for something bold, something clear, and something long overdue:

A total and complete ban on all foreign political donations and foreign lobbying efforts targeting the American political process.

Not a regulation. Not a disclosure requirement. Not a cap. A ban.

Here is why:

First, national security demands it. Foreign influence in our political system is not merely a theoretical concern — it is a documented, ongoing national security threat. Intelligence agencies from across the political spectrum have confirmed that foreign actors actively seek to manipulate American policy through financial influence. Safeguarding American Democracy: The Case for a Complete Ban on Foreign Political Donations and Lobbying

The United States was founded on a revolutionary principle: that political power derives from the consent of the governed. Embedded in this principle is an unstated but essential corollary—that "the governed" means the American people themselves, not foreign powers seeking to shape American policy for their own ends. Yet today, the channels through which foreign money and influence flow into the American political system remain alarmingly porous. A complete ban on all political donations and lobbying activities by foreign entities—whether corporations, individuals, or governments—is not merely a policy preference but an urgent necessity for preserving the integrity of American democracy.

The Constitutional and Historical Foundation

The Founding Fathers were acutely aware of the dangers posed by foreign influence. George Washington, in his Farewell Address, warned against "the insidious wiles of foreign influence," declaring it "one of the most baneful foes of republican government." The Constitution's Emoluments Clause explicitly prohibits federal officials from accepting gifts from foreign states without congressional consent—a clear recognition that foreign money in American politics is inherently corrupting.

This is not xenophobia; it is common sense. Self-governance loses its meaning when outside powers can purchase access, influence legislation, and shape electoral outcomes. The very concept of democratic sovereignty demands that a nation's political decisions emerge from its own citizens' deliberations, free from the financial pressures of those whose loyalties and interests lie elsewhere.

The Current Legal Landscape Is Insufficient

While the Federal Election Campaign Act prohibits direct contributions from foreign nationals to candidates and parties, this prohibition is riddled with loopholes. Foreign-owned domestic subsidiaries can establish political action committees. Foreign individuals can fund "issue advocacy" that stops just short of express electoral advocacy. Wealthy foreign interests can channel money through opaque nonprofit organizations that engage in substantial political activity without disclosing donors. And the lobbying industry—one of the most powerful forces shaping American legislation—remains wide open to foreign governments and corporations willing to pay American firms millions of dollars to advocate on their behalf.

The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), intended to provide transparency about foreign lobbying, has been notoriously under-enforced for decades. Registration is often delayed, ignored, or circumvented. Meanwhile, foreign governments spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually to shape American foreign policy, trade relationships, and regulatory decisions. The status quo treats foreign influence as a disclosure problem when it is, in truth, a sovereignty problem.

The Conflict of Interest Is Inescapable

When a foreign government hires former American officials to lobby their former colleagues, an inherent conflict arises. When a foreign corporation funds think tanks that produce "independent" research shaping congressional debates, the marketplace of ideas becomes contaminated by undisclosed interests. When foreign nationals use legal or quasi-legal channels to influence American elections, every vote cast on the basis of that influenced discourse is, to some degree, a vote cast under false pretenses.

American policymaking must answer to American citizens. A senator voting on tariffs, a representative weighing defense appropriations, or a regulator determining telecommunications rules should be responsive to the interests of their constituents—not to whichever foreign power has spent the most on sophisticated influence campaigns. Even the appearance of such influence erodes public trust, feeding the cynicism that hollows out democratic institutions from within.

National Security Implications

Beyond questions of democratic theory, foreign political influence poses direct national security risks. Hostile powers have demonstrated repeatedly their willingness to exploit open political systems to advance their strategic aims. Intelligence agencies have documented sustained campaigns by adversarial governments to shape American public opinion, cultivate sympathetic politicians, and steer policy in directions favorable to their geopolitical goals.

Even allied nations have interests that diverge from America's. Foreign lobbying on arms sales, trade agreements, and diplomatic recognition often serves foreign governments at the expense of American strategic priorities. The distinction between "friendly" and "hostile" foreign influence is less important than the fundamental principle: American policy should be made by and for Americans.

Responding to Objections

Critics may argue that banning all foreign political spending and lobbying would impede legitimate communication between nations and harm diplomatic relations. This argument conflates diplomacy with influence peddling. Foreign governments already possess proper channels for communicating with American officials: their embassies, the State Department, multilateral institutions, and direct government-to-government contacts. These formal channels are transparent and accountable. What a ban would eliminate is the shadow diplomacy conducted through paid American intermediaries, opaque funding networks, and indirect electoral pressure.

Others may invoke free speech concerns. But the First Amendment protects the rights of the American people to engage in self-governance; it was never intended as a shield for foreign powers seeking to manipulate American democracy. The Supreme Court has consistently recognized that the government's compelling interest in preventing foreign influence justifies restrictions that would be impermissible if applied to American citizens. A complete ban on foreign political spending is fully consistent with constitutional principles.

The Path Forward

A comprehensive ban should include several elements: prohibiting all political contributions—direct or indirect—from foreign nationals, foreign corporations, and foreign governments; closing the subsidiary loophole by barring political spending from any corporation with significant foreign ownership; ending paid foreign lobbying entirely, replacing it with transparent diplomatic channels; requiring exhaustive disclosure of any remaining foreign-linked political activity with criminal penalties for violations; and establishing a dedicated enforcement body with the resources and mandate to investigate and prosecute violations aggressively.

Such reforms would not isolate America from the world. Trade, diplomacy, cultural exchange, and scholarly dialogue would continue and flourish. What would end is the corrosive practice of allowing foreign wealth to shape American self-government.

Conclusion

Democracy is not a permanent condition but a fragile achievement requiring constant defense. The Founders understood that foreign influence represented one of the gravest threats to the republic they created. In an era of global capital flows, multinational corporations, and sophisticated influence operations, that threat has only intensified. A complete ban on foreign political donations and lobbying activities is a necessary measure to ensure that American democracy remains what it was always meant to be: government of, by, and for the American people. Anything less concedes a portion of our sovereignty to those who have not earned it and whose interests are not our own.

Model Response:

The United States should impose a complete ban on political donations and lobbying by any foreign entities—foreign corporations, individuals, and governments—to safeguard the core democratic principle of self-government. Democracy rests on a simple premise: the people who live under the laws should be the ones who shape them. Allowing foreign money and organized influence into our political system erodes that premise, misaligns public policy with the will of the governed, and invites strategic manipulation by actors whose interests may diverge sharply from America’s.

This principle already has strong constitutional footing. U.S. law bans foreign nationals from contributing to candidates, parties, and political committees, and courts have upheld that restriction on the basis that foreign citizens have no right to participate in the nation’s processes of democratic self-government. Yet the current framework is incomplete. It is riddled with loopholes that allow foreign money to seep into the system through shell companies, straw donors, and opaque nonprofits, and it treats foreign lobbying as a disclosure problem rather than a democratic integrity problem. A categorical ban on both political donations and lobbying by foreign entities would close these gaps with a clean line: no foreign money, and no foreign-directed advocacy, in American politics.

The status quo illustrates why a partial approach fails. Federal law prohibits foreign contributions to electoral committees, but enforcement struggles against the speed and complexity of modern finance. Dark-money vehicles such as 501(c)(4) organizations can accept funds without disclosing donors, making it difficult to ensure foreign-origin money is not indirectly buying influence in elections or ballot initiatives. U.S.-based subsidiaries of foreign corporations can spend in politics if the funds and decision-making are kept onshore, but those “firewalls” are notoriously hard to verify. And while the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) requires agents of foreign principals to register and disclose their activities, it does not stop those activities; it simply puts them on a form. Foreign governments and companies can—and do—hire lobbyists to press their strategic and commercial agendas on Capitol Hill and in the executive branch.

This is not a hypothetical concern. Recent years have exposed a string of cases where foreign money sought to penetrate American politics via straw donors and unregistered influence campaigns. Even when enforcement succeeds after the fact, the damage is done: access is granted, policy is nudged, and public trust is diminished. Nor is the problem limited to adversaries. Friendly nations and multinational corporations pursue their interests rationally; sometimes those interests conflict with those of U.S. workers, consumers, or national security. When foreign principals can deploy money and professional advocates to shape American rulemaking, procurement, trade, and technology policy, democratic accountability is diluted.

A complete ban advances three compelling goals.

First, it protects sovereignty and democratic self-determination. The American polity should not be steered by foreign financial leverage. Citizens, not overseas shareholders or ministries, must define the public interest. A blanket prohibition draws a bright, enforceable line consistent with constitutional principles already recognized in election law.

Second, it mitigates national security risks. Foreign political influence is a cost-effective instrument of statecraft; it is far cheaper to sway legislation than to develop military capabilities. Barring foreign lobbying and donations reduces the attack surface for strategic influence, covert or overt, and removes incentives to exploit our openness through front groups and proxies.

Third, it promotes fairness and economic integrity. Policy should be shaped by the merits of arguments accessible to all, not by who can finance the most seasoned lobbyists or route funds through the most sophisticated compliance structures. Domestic actors remain fully free to petition government; foreign principals should not be able to tilt the playing field in ways that distort markets or regulatory outcomes to the disadvantage of American communities.

Critics raise three main objections, none persuasive.

They argue that lobbying supplies expertise to policymakers. Expertise is not the issue; the pay-to-influence model is. Policymakers can and should obtain information through hearings, advisory bodies, public rulemaking dockets, independent research, and diplomatic channels for foreign governments. A ban targets the transactional advocacy industry that sells access and pressure, not the flow of knowledge itself.

They warn of free-speech concerns. But the First Amendment’s strongest protections attach to the speech and political participation of the domestic political community. Courts have already affirmed that foreign nationals may be barred from financing electoral advocacy. Extending that principle to paid lobbying by foreign principals advances a compelling interest in democratic integrity, without chilling the speech of U.S. citizens and permanent residents acting in their personal capacity.

They fear retaliation against U.S. interests abroad. Many democracies—including the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia—already restrict or ban foreign political donations and have tightened rules on foreign influence. A clear, principled U.S. standard is likely to harmonize rather than escalate norms, and it positions America to advocate globally for cleaner democratic practices.

A categorical ban should be paired with practical implementation to make it effective and fair:

  • Define “foreign entity” by ultimate beneficial ownership and control, not just place of incorporation, to prevent shell company workarounds.
  • Prohibit direct and indirect political donations from foreign sources across the board: candidates, parties, super PACs, 501(c)(4)s, 527s, ballot measure committees, and inaugural or transition entities. Outlaw in-kind support such as staff time, research, and data.
  • Ban lobbying by or on behalf of foreign principals at the federal, state, and local levels. Individuals may still speak as private citizens, but not as agents or employees advancing a foreign principal’s policy agenda for pay.
  • Require robust due diligence by recipients, including banks, political committees, and nonprofits, with strict liability for accepting foreign funds and meaningful penalties for violations.
  • Mandate beneficial-ownership transparency for entities engaging with politics, real-time disclosure of large donations from domestic sources, and routine audits to deter and detect evasion.
  • Close the subsidiary loophole: U.S. affiliates controlled by foreign parents may not spend in politics or hire lobbyists to influence U.S. policy, regardless of internal firewalls. If a foreign principal stands to benefit and directs the effort, it is prohibited.
  • Impose strong sanctions: disgorgement, treble penalties, debarment from federal contracts, and criminal liability for willful schemes, along with a private right of action to empower civil enforcement.

Crucially, such a ban does not isolate the United States or cut policymakers off from global realities. Diplomats will continue to engage through established channels; agencies will continue to receive public comments and expert testimony; research and journalism will continue to inform debate. What changes is that foreign money and paid advocacy will no longer be the currency of influence in our domestic political process.

A democracy that cannot police the border between self-government and purchased foreign leverage will eventually lose both public trust and policy independence. A complete ban on foreign political donations and lobbying is not a gesture of hostility to the world; it is an act of democratic hygiene. It tells citizens that their voices, not foreign checkbooks, set the nation’s course. And it tells the world that America’s laws are written by and for the American people alone.

And a people who must compete against hidden, foreign‑financed campaigns are not being heard on equal terms. We cannot tiptoe around this. If our votes are sacred, so must be the process that surrounds them.

Some will say, “But we already have restrictions.” Yes, we do. And we have loopholes big enough to fly a cargo plane through. Foreign funds can filter through U.S. subsidiaries. They can be laundered through “social welfare” organizations that never disclose their donors. They can bankroll “issue ads” that stop just short of naming a candidate but fully aim to sway an election. They can hire compliant intermediaries to lobby our officials while claiming it’s all perfectly legal. This is influence laundering—and it must end.

Outlawing foreign political donations and lobbying means making a series of clear, common‑sense commitments:

  • No foreign money—zero—in our elections, at any level, in any form. Not to candidates, not to parties, not to super PACs, not to ballot initiatives, not to “issue advocacy,” not to influencers or digital ad networks. If the source is foreign, the answer is no.

  • No lobbying on behalf of any foreign government, foreign political party, state‑owned enterprise, or foreign‑controlled corporation. No backdoor consulting, no “strategic advising,” no law firm fig leaves. If you are paid by a foreign principal to influence U.S. policy, you cannot do it—period.

  • Full transparency of real beneficial ownership. No more shell games. If money touches our politics, we must know who truly stands behind it. If a U.S. entity is foreign‑controlled, then the money is foreign—end of story.

  • End the dark money ecosystem. Require real‑time disclosure for significant political spending, strict audits, and tough penalties that actually deter. Sunlight is a disinfectant; let’s open the windows.

  • Guardrails for the digital age. Verify political advertisers, trace funding sources, and label content so voters know who is talking to them. Bots and sock puppets do not get a say in our republic.

  • Enforce the law with teeth. Give regulators and prosecutors the resources and authority to investigate, subpoena, and punish. The cost of getting caught should vastly exceed the benefit of trying.

This is not about immigrants or Americans with family abroad. This is not about your heritage, your accent, or your passport once you become a citizen. This is about money and power—about preventing foreign states and foreign‑controlled entities from using cash to bend our system. We welcome people from every corner of the earth to join our national story. But no government, no party, and no boardroom beyond our borders gets to bankroll the writing of our laws.

Some will argue that foreign lobbying is merely “information.” But diplomacy has a proper home: open, official channels between governments, conducted on the record and accountable to the public. The marketplace of ideas is for our people; the marketplace of influence is not for sale to foreign bidders. Others will whisper that such a ban could cost jobs for lobbyists and consultants. If the price of those jobs is our sovereignty, then that price is too high.

We should also be honest: this change will not solve every problem in our politics. We still must confront domestic corruption, concentrated wealth, and the corrosive influence of unlimited spending. But drawing a bright red line against foreign money is the floor of self‑respect for a free people. It says to the world—and to ourselves—that America’s voice is not for rent.

Congress should pass a comprehensive law that bans foreign political spending and foreign lobbying in all forms and closes every known loophole. States should mirror and reinforce those protections for their own elections and ballot measures. Agencies should update rules for the digital era and prosecute violators with vigor. Think tanks, universities, and nonprofits should disclose foreign funding and refuse it when it touches public policy advocacy. And candidates—of every party—should take a simple pledge: we will accept no foreign‑linked funds, directly or indirectly, and we will reject lobbying from foreign principals.

But most of all, this is a job for citizens. Demand these reforms. Ask every candidate where they stand. Support leaders who choose sovereignty over convenience, and transparency over access. Make it known that we will no longer tolerate a politics where the loudest checks write the loudest speeches.

Our forebears fought a revolution to decide for themselves who governs them. They did not risk their lives so that centuries later our choices could be quietly bartered away in conference rooms bought with foreign money. We honor them not with nostalgia, but with resolve. Let us build a firewall of law and principle so sturdy that no foreign treasury can breach it. Let us say, with one clear voice: the American people write America’s future.

Our votes are not for sale. Our laws are not for lease. Our country is not a client state.

Let us outlaw foreign political donations and lobbying, and let us do it now—so that our children inherit a democracy that is wholly, undeniably, and proudly our own.

Sovereignty for Sale: The Case for a Total Ban on Foreign Political Donations and Lobbying in U.S. Democracy

Introduction

The United States of America was founded on a revolutionary principle: that a nation's government should derive its legitimacy and direction from the consent of its own governed people. Yet today, this foundational covenant is under sustained assault—not by armies or navies, but by checkbooks, wire transfers, and influence operations orchestrated by foreign entities seeking to bend American policy toward their own interests. While existing laws nominally restrict direct foreign contributions to political campaigns, these laws are riddled with loopholes, weakened by inadequate enforcement, and fundamentally insufficient in scope. The time has come for the United States to enact a comprehensive, unequivocal ban on all political donations and lobbying activities by foreign entities—whether foreign governments, foreign corporations, or foreign individuals—to preserve the basic democratic principle that American policy should be made by Americans, for Americans.

This is not a partisan argument. It is a structural argument about the architecture of self-governance. Whether one sits on the political left or right, whether one favors an expansive or limited federal government, the premise that a democratic republic must be insulated from external financial manipulation should be axiomatic. Foreign influence in domestic politics is not free speech; it is an intrusion upon sovereignty. It is not diplomacy; it is subversion conducted through legal gray areas. And it is not simply a theoretical concern; it is a documented, ongoing, and escalating threat.

I. The Current Legal Framework Is Dangerously Inadequate

Federal law already prohibits direct contributions from foreign nationals to federal, state, or local elections under the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA), as amended, and further codified under 52 U.S.C. § 30121. The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), enacted in 1938 in response to Nazi propaganda operations in the United States, requires individuals acting as agents of foreign principals to register with the Department of Justice and disclose their activities. On paper, these laws appear robust. In practice, they are alarmingly porous.

The lobbying loophole is perhaps the most consequential weakness. While FARA requires registration for those acting under the direct control of foreign governments, the Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) of 1995 created a parallel—and far less stringent—registration regime. In practice, many individuals and firms representing foreign interests register under the LDA rather than FARA, thereby avoiding the more rigorous disclosure requirements and the stigma associated with being labeled a "foreign agent." A 2016 report by the Project on Government Oversight (POGO) found that FARA enforcement had been so lax for decades that the Department of Justice had brought only a handful of criminal prosecutions since the law's inception. The result is a system in which foreign interests can effectively purchase access to American lawmakers while operating in a regulatory twilight zone.

Moreover, the rise of globalized corporate structures has made the prohibition on foreign campaign contributions easy to circumvent. U.S. subsidiaries of foreign corporations can establish political action committees (PACs) and make contributions using domestically generated revenue, even though the parent company—and therefore the ultimate decision-making authority—is headquartered abroad and answers to foreign shareholders and, in some cases, foreign governments. The legal fiction that a U.S. subsidiary is entirely independent in its political activities from its foreign parent defies both common sense and the observable realities of corporate governance.

Dark money channels present yet another vulnerability. Foreign funds can be funneled through 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations and other nonprofit entities that are not required to disclose their donors. While these organizations are technically prohibited from having political activity as their primary purpose, the IRS definition of "primary" has proven extraordinarily elastic, and enforcement has been virtually nonexistent. The result is that millions of dollars of untraceable origin flow into the American political system every election cycle, and there is no reliable mechanism to ensure that none of this money originates from foreign sources.

A comprehensive ban would close these loopholes not by attempting to patch each one individually—an approach that has repeatedly failed—but by establishing a clear, categorical prohibition: no foreign entity, directly or indirectly, may spend money to influence American political outcomes. Period.

II. Foreign Lobbying Distorts American Policy to Serve External Interests

The argument for a total ban gains its most compelling force from examining the tangible consequences of foreign lobbying on American policy. When foreign governments and corporations spend billions of dollars to shape U.S. legislation, regulation, and diplomatic posture, the results are predictable: American policy shifts to accommodate foreign interests, often at the direct expense of American citizens, workers, and national security.

Consider the scale of the enterprise. According to the Center for Responsive Politics and subsequent analyses by OpenSecrets, foreign governments and entities spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually on lobbying activities in Washington. Saudi Arabia, for instance, has spent tens of millions of dollars on lobbying and public relations firms in the United States, particularly during periods when its human rights record—including the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi and the devastating military campaign in Yemen—placed it under Congressional scrutiny. The objective of this spending is transparent: to prevent or weaken legislative actions that would impose consequences on the Saudi government for its behavior. When such lobbying succeeds, it means that American foreign policy has been, in effect, purchased—that the moral and strategic judgments of elected representatives have been overridden by foreign money.

China presents an equally concerning case. Through a complex web of state-owned enterprises, nominally private companies with deep government ties, and cultural and educational organizations, the Chinese government has built an extensive influence infrastructure within the United States. Defense contractors from allied nations lobby aggressively for weapons procurement contracts, potentially steering the U.S. military toward equipment that serves the commercial interests of foreign manufacturers rather than the operational requirements of American service members. Foreign pharmaceutical companies lobby against drug pricing reforms that would benefit American consumers. Foreign agricultural interests lobby against trade protections for American farmers. In each case, the dynamic is the same: foreign money purchases access, access produces influence, and influence translates into policy outcomes that serve foreign interests at America's expense.

Defenders of the current system argue that lobbying provides lawmakers with valuable information and expertise. This argument is not without merit in the domestic context, where American citizens and organizations have a legitimate interest in communicating their views to their elected representatives. But foreign entities are not constituents. They do not vote. They do not bear the consequences of the policies they seek to influence. Their participation in the policy process is not an exercise of democratic rights; it is an exercise of financial power by actors whose interests are, by definition, external to the American polity. Information that foreign governments wish to communicate to American lawmakers can be conveyed through established diplomatic channels—through embassies, consulates, and the Department of State—without requiring the apparatus of K Street lobbying firms, lavish fundraising events, and revolving-door hiring practices.

III. The Revolving Door Amplifies Foreign Influence to Dangerous Levels

No discussion of foreign influence in American politics would be complete without addressing the revolving door between government service and foreign lobbying. The phenomenon is bipartisan, widespread, and deeply corrosive to public trust.

Former members of Congress, retired generals and admirals, ex-cabinet officials, and senior congressional staffers routinely transition into lucrative positions with lobbying firms that represent foreign governments. They bring with them not only their policy expertise and institutional knowledge—which are valuable in any employment context—but their personal relationships with sitting lawmakers, their understanding of internal legislative processes, and, in many cases, their security clearances. When a former senator picks up the phone to call a current senator on behalf of a foreign government client, the conversation carries a weight and intimacy that no ordinary lobbyist could replicate. The foreign government is not merely purchasing advocacy; it is purchasing the social capital accumulated over years of public service.

This phenomenon has been extensively documented. Exposed foreign lobbying client lists have revealed that former senior officials from both parties have represented governments with interests directly contrary to stated U.S. policy. Former officials have lobbied on behalf of governments subject to U.S. sanctions, governments accused of human rights abuses, and governments actively working to undermine American strategic interests in key regions. The fact that such work is legal—provided that the appropriate registrations are filed, which they often are not—represents a systemic failure of the current regulatory framework.

A comprehensive ban on foreign lobbying would sever this pipeline entirely. Former government officials would remain free to enter the private sector, to consult, to teach, to write, and to engage in any number of productive post-government careers. What they would not be able to do is monetize their public service on behalf of foreign powers. This restriction is not punitive; it is prophylactic. It protects the integrity of government service by ensuring that officials make decisions based on the national interest rather than on the anticipation of future lobbying income.

IV. The National Security Imperative

The national security argument for a comprehensive ban is perhaps the most straightforward and the most urgent. Foreign influence operations are not merely a matter of domestic political concern; they are a recognized tool of geopolitical competition.

The intelligence community's assessment of Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election brought this issue into sharp public focus, but the problem extends far beyond any single election or any single adversary. China, Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Turkey, and numerous other nations have been identified as conducting influence operations targeting the United States through various means, including political donations (often disguised or laundered), lobbying, media manipulation, and cultivation of personal relationships with American officials.

The current legal framework treats these activities as distinct categories, subject to different regulatory regimes with different enforcement mechanisms. A foreign government's intelligence service recruiting an American official as a spy is treated as espionage—a serious federal crime. But the same foreign government hiring a prominent Washington lobbying firm to achieve similar policy outcomes through legal advocacy is treated as a routine commercial transaction, subject only to disclosure requirements that are widely flouted. This distinction makes no strategic sense. From the perspective of the foreign government, both activities serve the same objective: shaping American behavior to serve foreign interests. The method differs; the intent and the effect do not.

A comprehensive ban would eliminate this artificial distinction by recognizing that all foreign efforts to influence American political outcomes through financial means—whether covert or overt, whether conducted through intelligence operatives or through registered lobbyists—represent an intrusion upon American sovereignty that should not be tolerated.

Critics may argue that such a ban would be difficult to enforce. This is true, but it is an argument for investing in enforcement capacity, not for abandoning the prohibition. The United States does not decline to criminalize fraud simply because fraud is difficult to detect. The existence of a clear legal prohibition creates a framework for investigation and prosecution, empowers enforcement agencies, and establishes social and professional norms that deter violations. Under the current system, many foreign influence activities are technically legal, which means that enforcement agencies have no basis for action even when the activities are identified. A comprehensive ban would change this calculus fundamentally.

V. Answering the Objections

Opponents of a comprehensive ban raise several objections that deserve serious consideration—and serious rebuttal.

"A ban would violate the First Amendment." This objection, while superficially plausible, does not withstand scrutiny. The First Amendment protects the rights of Americans to speak, to assemble, and to petition their government. It has never been understood to guarantee foreign governments, foreign corporations, or foreign nationals a right to spend money to influence American elections or legislation. Even the Supreme Court's expansive reading of the First Amendment in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010) explicitly preserved the prohibition on foreign contributions to elections, with Justice Kennedy's majority opinion noting that the government has a compelling interest in preventing foreign influence. A comprehensive ban on foreign lobbying and political spending would extend this recognized principle to its logical conclusion.

"A ban would harm international commerce and diplomacy." This objection conflates distinct activities. International trade, investment, and diplomatic engagement are not dependent on the ability of foreign entities to lobby Congress or contribute to political campaigns. Foreign governments would remain free to engage with the U.S. government through normal diplomatic channels. Foreign corporations would remain free to operate in the United States, to hire American workers, to sell products to American consumers, and to comply with American regulations. What they would not be able to do is spend money to shape those regulations in their favor through the political process. This is not a restriction on commerce; it is a restriction on political manipulation.

"A ban would be unenforceable." As noted above, enforceability is a question of resources and political will, not of principle. The United States maintains extensive regulatory frameworks governing financial transactions, including the Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering statutes, and the Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctions regime. These frameworks provide the investigative tools necessary to trace foreign funds. What is lacking is the legal framework that would make the mere act of foreign political spending—regardless of whether it is disclosed—a violation of law. A comprehensive ban would provide this framework.

"Other countries allow foreign lobbying, and a unilateral ban would put the U.S. at a disadvantage." This argument inverts the logic of sovereignty. The fact that other nations may tolerate foreign influence in their political systems is not a reason for the United States to do the same. If anything, the opposite is true: a nation that insulates its political process from foreign financial manipulation is stronger, not weaker, in its dealings with other nations. It is precisely because the United States is a global superpower with outsized influence over international affairs that foreign entities are willing to spend so lavishly to shape its policies. A ban would ensure that this influence remains in American hands.

VI. A Blueprint for Reform

A comprehensive ban should include the following elements:

First, a categorical prohibition on all political contributions, donations, and expenditures by foreign governments, foreign political parties, foreign corporations (including U.S. subsidiaries of foreign-owned companies above a defined ownership threshold), and foreign nationals. This prohibition should extend to all elections—federal, state, and local—and to all forms of political spending, including independent expenditures, contributions to PACs and Super PACs, and donations to 501(c)(4) organizations engaged in political activity.

Second, a categorical prohibition on all lobbying of federal and state officials by or on behalf of foreign governments and foreign political parties. Foreign corporations should be permitted to engage with regulatory agencies on compliance matters directly affecting their U.S. operations, but should be prohibited from lobbying on legislative matters.

Third, the elimination of the LDA as an alternative registration regime for those acting on behalf of foreign principals. All such individuals should be required to register under a strengthened FARA, with robust disclosure requirements, regular compliance audits, and meaningful penalties for violations.

Fourth, a lifetime ban on former senior government officials—including members of Congress, Senate-confirmed officials, and general and flag officers—engaging in any compensated activity on behalf of foreign governments.

Fifth, the establishment of a dedicated enforcement unit within the Department of Justice, with sufficient resources and independence to investigate and prosecute violations.

Sixth, mandatory disclosure of the ultimate beneficial ownership of all entities making political contributions, to prevent the use of shell companies and intermediary organizations to launder foreign funds.

Conclusion

The integrity of American democracy is not a partisan issue, a liberal issue, or a conservative issue. It is the foundational issue upon which all other political questions rest. If American policy can be purchased by the highest foreign bidder, then elections are mere theater, and self-governance is an illusion.

The United States faces genuine adversaries who seek to weaken its institutions and divide its people. It also engages with allies and partners whose interests, while often aligned with America's, are not identical. In neither case is it appropriate for foreign entities to wield financial influence over the American political process. Adversaries will use such influence to subvert; allies will use it to extract concessions. In both cases, the American people lose.

A comprehensive ban on foreign political donations and lobbying is not radical. It is the logical extension of principles that are already embedded in American law and American political philosophy. It is the recognition that sovereignty means something—that the right of a people to govern themselves is not merely a slogan but a commitment that must be actively defended against those who would undermine it with money.

The Founders understood the danger of foreign influence. In his Farewell Address, George Washington warned that "foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government." Alexander Hamilton, in Federalist No. 68, praised the Electoral College in part because it would protect against "the desire in foreign powers to gain an improper ascendant in our councils." James Madison, in designing the constitutional architecture of checks and balances, sought to create a government that would be responsive to its own citizens and resistant to external manipulation.

Two and a half centuries later, the threat that the Founders identified has not diminished; it has metastasized. The tools of foreign influence are more sophisticated, the sums of money are larger, the legal channels are more numerous, and the enforcement mechanisms are weaker. The answer is not to surrender to this reality but to confront it—clearly, comprehensively, and without exception.

The American people deserve a government that answers to them. A total ban on foreign political donations and lobbying would not guarantee such a government, but it would remove one of the most powerful mechanisms by which that guarantee is currently being eroded. It is time to act—not with half-measures and incremental reforms, but with the clarity and conviction that the defense of self-governance demands.

DEFENDING THE REPUBLIC: A SPEECH ON FOREIGN INFLUENCE IN AMERICAN POLITICS

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow Americans,

There is a principle so fundamental to the very idea of self-governance that our Founders considered it self-evident — that the people of a nation, and only the people of that nation, should determine its course. Tonight, I stand before you to talk about a threat to that principle — not one that arrives with armies or warships, but one that arrives with wire transfers, consulting contracts, and quiet dinners in Washington restaurants.

I am speaking about foreign political donations and foreign lobbying in the halls of American government — and I am here to make the case, plainly and without apology, that both should be outlawed completely and enforced aggressively.

Let me be clear about what we are discussing. Right now, as we speak, foreign governments, foreign corporations, and foreign interests spend billions of dollars attempting to shape American law, American foreign policy, and American elections. They hire former senators. They hire former cabinet officials. They fund think tanks that produce studies miraculously aligned with their benefactor's interests. They exploit loopholes in our campaign finance system wide enough to sail a cargo ship through. And they do much of it legally — because we have allowed a system to develop that treats the influence of foreign powers over our democracy as just another line of business.

This is not democracy. This is an auction.

Think about what self-governance actually means. When an American citizen votes, they carry with them the weight of a sacred trust — the trust that their voice, aggregated with millions of other American voices, will chart the direction of this country. Every time a foreign government successfully lobbies a member of Congress, every time foreign money finds its way into our political ecosystem, that trust is diluted. That vote is cheapened. That citizen's sovereignty — your sovereignty — is compromised.

And let no one dismiss this as a partisan concern. This is not about left or right. Foreign influence does not respect party lines. It targets whoever is useful. It courts Democrats and Republicans with equal enthusiasm. Authoritarian regimes, rival economic powers, and even allied nations all engage in efforts to bend American policy toward their interests and away from yours. The question is not whether it is happening. The question is why we still tolerate it.

Now, some will argue — and they argue persuasively in the salons and boardrooms where these arrangements are made — that foreign lobbying is simply "diplomacy by other means," that it promotes mutual understanding, that banning it would isolate us from the world.

I reject that argument entirely.

Diplomacy happens between governments, through official channels, with transparency and accountability. What we are talking about is something very different. We are talking about retired American officials registering as agents of foreign powers and using their relationships, their access, and their insider knowledge to advance another nation's agenda — often against the interests of the American people they once swore to serve. We are talking about shell corporations funneling money into super PACs. We are talking about a revolving door that spins so fast it generates its own gravitational pull.

That is not diplomacy. That is infiltration by checkbook.

And let us talk about the lobbying itself. Under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — FARA — foreign agents are technically required to register and disclose their activities. But FARA, as currently enforced, is a paper tiger with no teeth and no claws. For decades, enforcement has been sporadic at best, negligent at worst. Thousands of individuals who should be registered are not. Penalties are rarely imposed. The Department of Justice has treated FARA more as a filing requirement than as the national security statute it was designed to be when it was passed in 1938 — in response, let us remember, to Nazi propaganda operations on American soil.

Our forebears saw the danger clearly enough to act. Have we become so complacent, so comfortable, that we can no longer see what they saw?

Here is what I propose, and I do not propose it lightly:

First — a complete ban on political donations from any foreign source, whether direct or indirect, with criminal penalties for both the giver and the receiver. No loopholes. No subsidiaries. No intermediaries. If the money originates from a foreign interest, it has no place in American politics. Period.

Second — an end to foreign government lobbying of Congress and federal agencies through paid private agents. If a foreign government wishes to communicate its position to the United States, it may do so through its embassy, through its diplomats, through the established channels of international relations — not through K Street firms billing six hundred dollars an hour.

Third — a lifetime ban on former senior government officials — presidents, cabinet secretaries, members of Congress, senior intelligence and military officials — from ever registering as agents of a foreign power. You served America. Your loyalty should not be for sale to the highest bidder when you leave office. The door should be closed, locked, and welded shut.

Fourth — the creation of a dedicated, independent enforcement body with real investigative power, real prosecutorial authority, and real resources. Not a suggestion box. Not an understaffed office in the basement of the Department of Justice. A serious institution for a serious threat.

"But this will hurt international business," they will say. "This will strain alliances," they will warn. "This is impractical," they will object.

Let me address each of those concerns directly.

International business does not require corrupting our political process. Companies around the world do business in the United States every single day without needing to buy a senator. If your business model depends on purchasing political influence in a foreign country, then your business model is the problem — not our laws.

As for our alliances — true allies do not need to secretly manipulate our politics. True allies engage with us honestly, government to government, with mutual respect. Any alliance that depends on covert influence operations is not an alliance at all. It is a dependency.

And as for practicality — we put men on the moon. We built the most sophisticated intelligence apparatus in the history of the world. Do not tell me we cannot track wire transfers. Do not tell me we cannot enforce disclosure laws. We can. We have simply lacked the will.

Let me tell you what is truly impractical. It is impractical to maintain a democratic republic while allowing foreign powers to purchase influence within it. History is littered with the ruins of nations that allowed outside powers to corrupt their internal politics. The late Roman Republic. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The republics of Renaissance Italy. In every case, foreign gold accelerated domestic decay. In every case, citizens woke up one day to find that the decisions being made in their name were being made for someone else's benefit.

We are not combating with this problem. We are inviting it. And every year we fail to act, the roots grow deeper, the relationships grow more entrenched, and the web grows more complex.

My fellow Americans, I want to speak to you not as a policy matter now, but as a matter of principle — of national honor.

This country was born in revolution against a distant power that presumed to govern us without our consent. "No taxation without representation" was not merely an economic slogan. It was a moral declaration — that the people who live under a government must be the people who control it. That principle did not expire with the Treaty of Paris in 1783. It did not become obsolete with globalization. It is not a relic. It is the foundation.

Every foreign dollar that enters our political system is a vote cast by someone who bears none of the consequences of our laws. Every foreign lobbying campaign that shapes our legislation is a hand on the wheel that has no right to steer. And every American official who sells their influence to a foreign government after leaving office is committing a betrayal of the public trust that should shock our conscience — even if it does not currently violate our laws.

We must make it violate our laws.

I am not naive. I understand that in a connected world, nations influence each other. I understand that information flows across borders and that global challenges require cooperation. I am not calling for isolation. I am not calling for xenophobia. I am calling for something far simpler and far more American:

I am calling for integrity.

I am calling for a political system where every dollar is accountable, every influence is transparent, and every decision is made by people who answer to the American voter — not to foreign capitals, foreign corporations, or foreign princes.

This is not radical. In fact, it is the minimum requirement of genuine sovereignty. A nation that cannot control who influences its own government is not truly sovereign at all. It merely has the appearance of sovereignty — the flag, the anthem, the buildings — while the substance is hollowed out from within.

We deserve better than that. We — the mechanics and the teachers, the nurses and the farmers, the veterans and the students, the people who live under these laws and fight under this flag — we deserve a political process that belongs to us.

Not to the highest foreign bidder.

Not to the cleverest lobbyist.

Not to the most well-connected former official peddling access.

To us.

So I call upon the Congress of the United States to act — not next session, not after the next election, not after yet another study or commission or report. Now. Pass legislation that bans foreign political donations absolutely. Pass legislation that ends the foreign lobbying industry as it currently exists. Pass legislation that slams shut the revolving door between public service and foreign agency. And fund the enforcement mechanisms to make these laws more than words on paper.

And I call upon every American to demand it. Call your representatives. Write your senators. Make this a litmus test. Make this a condition. Because if we do not protect our own political process, no one else will do it for us. No one.

The Founders pledged their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor to create a nation governed by its own people. The least we can do — the very least — is ensure that the nation they built is not sold out from under us by those who see our democracy not as a sacred trust, but as a market opportunity.

Let us close the door. Let us protect what is ours. Let us remind the world — and remind ourselves — that the United States of America governs itself.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.
